content: A diketone is a molecule that contains two ketone functional groups. The simplest example of a diketone is diacetyl, also referred to as 2,3-butanedione. Specific examples of diketones include 2,3-butanedione, acetylacetone, and hexane-2,5-dione, which represent 1,2-, 1,3-, and 1,4-diketones, respectively. Dimedone, chemically known as 5,5-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexanedione (CAS registry number 126-81-8), is an example of a cyclic diketone. 1,3-Diketones, such as acetylacetone, are particularly prone to forming stable enol or enolate structures. This stability arises due to the conjugation of the enol or enolate with the adjacent carbonyl group, as well as the energetic advantage of forming a six-membered ring. In the case of enols, this ring is stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, while in enolates, it involves the counterion. The conjugate bases derived from 1,3-diketones are capable of forming complexes with metal ions. Diketones that have one or two methylene groups separating the carbonyl groups typically exist in equilibrium with their enol tautomers. The chemical reactions of such dicarbonyl compounds are generally similar to those of simple ketones. The European Union (EU) Commission has classified diketones, such as acetylacetone (CH3COCH2COCH3), as genotoxic substances both in vitro and in vivo. This classification places them in the same category as dialcohols and hydroxyketones. Consequently, diketones have been prohibited as nutritional additives since 2005. Diacetyl, being the simplest diketone, may also eventually fall under this EU regulation.
